stem: A client rescued from an enclosed-space fire has facial burns, hoarseness, stridor, and increasing work of breathing. What is the priority concern?

options.A: Progressive inhalation-related upper-airway edema requiring urgent airway assessment and possible early airway control
options.B: A cosmetic facial injury with no airway implications
options.C: An uncomplicated skin burn that can be assessed after discharge
options.D: Seasonal allergy as the most likely explanation for stridor after the fire

rationale: Inhalation injury can cause progressive upper-airway edema. Hoarseness, stridor, respiratory distress, and other airway-obstruction signs after smoke/fire exposure require urgent airway assessment; early airway control may be necessary before edema makes intubation more difficult. Facial burns or singed hair alone are not treated as absolute indications, so the item includes active airway findings.
educational_objective: Prioritize airway assessment when smoke-exposed burn clients show signs of evolving upper-airway compromise.
source_locator: History and Physical; Treatment/Management — stridor, airway compromise, early/preemptive intubation consideration
source_claim_supported: Supports concern for inhalation injury and urgent airway management when hoarseness/stridor/respiratory distress follow smoke exposure.
correction_summary: Strengthened the stem with active airway-compromise findings and avoided treating singed hair or soot alone as absolute intubation criteria.
audit_findings: A uniquely addresses the ABC priority; B-D ignore a potentially rapidly obstructing airway.
